extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and general readers interested in philosophy of science and Thomas Kuhn
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes Thomas Kuhn's account of scientific development (paradigms, normal science, revolutions, incommensurability) and the criteria he invokes for theory choice and paradigm assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory choice characteristics (Kuhn's five)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kuhn identifies five characteristics that provide the shared basis for a choice of theory: 1. accuracy; 2. consistency (both internal and with other relevant currently accepted theories); 3. scope (its consequences should extend beyond the data it is required to explain); 4. simplicity (organizing otherwise confused and isolated phenomena); 5. fruitfulness (for further research).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn treats these as constitutive features of science but stresses they cannot determine scientific choice: which features count, how to interpret them (e.g. simplicity of ontology vs mathematical form), their imprecision, and their relative weighting are all disputable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of a paradigm (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: A paradigm supplies puzzles for scientists to solve and provides the tools for their solution; paradigms include key theories, problem-solutions, and the techniques/instruments used in applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of paradigms include great texts (Ptolemy's Almagest, Lavoisier's Traité, Newton's Principia) which contain theories and exemplar applications; paradigms guide normal science by fixing problems and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm-as-exemplar functions (three explicit functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) it suggests new puzzles; (ii) it suggests approaches to solving those puzzles; (iii) it is the standard by which the quality of a proposed puzzle-solution can be measured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn emphasizes scientists' perception of similarity to exemplars as the guide: similarity to the exemplar governs which solutions are accepted; exemplars are models of exemplary science used in training and research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal science criterion: puzzle-solving and conservatism
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal science is characterized as 'puzzle-solving' where scientists work on familiar puzzles expecting solvability and do not seek to refute guiding theories; success depends on shared familiarity with puzzles and methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normal science requires a strong commitment to shared theoretical beliefs, techniques, instruments and values (the disciplinary matrix). Anomalies are typically ignored or explained away unless they accumulate into a crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary matrix composition and commitment requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A disciplinary matrix consists of key theories, instruments, values, techniques and metaphysical assumptions; commitment to this constellation is a pre-requisite for successful normal science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such commitment is inculcated in scientific training and forms the mind-set of successful scientists; the disciplinary matrix explains conservativeness and why revolutions are rare and not rule-governed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for a successful scientific revolution (replacement paradigm requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: A replacement paradigm must eliminate at least the most pressing anomalies, solve the majority of those puzzles, and retain much of the problem-solving power of its predecessor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn notes 'Kuhn-loss' (some achievements of the prior period may be lost). He clarifies that newer theories must retain almost all predecessor quantitative problem-solving power though they may lose some qualitative explanatory virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kuhn-loss (criterion regarding retained explanatory/problem-solving power)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific revolutions can involve loss of some previously available problem-solutions (Kuhn-loss); a worthwhile replacement must on balance increase puzzle-solving power despite any such losses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revolutions bring an overall increase in puzzle-solving power when the number and significance of puzzles solved by the revised paradigm exceed those lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of assessment are paradigm-dependent (not permanent rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgment of a theory's epistemic quality is made by comparison to a paradigmatic theory; standards of assessment are neither permanent nor theory-independent rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because paradigms change, the measures used to evaluate puzzle-solutions change as well; what counts as an objection in one paradigm may not in another (e.g., role of 'mechanism' in Newtonian vs later contexts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of incommensurability
rubrics_metrics.description: Kuhn distinguishes three types of incommensurability: (1) methodological — no common measure because methods of comparison and evaluation change; (2) perceptual/observational — observational evidence cannot provide a common basis because perception is theory-dependent; (3) semantic — languages of theories may not be inter-translatable, shifting meanings of key terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These varieties explain why theory-comparison can be difficult or in some cases impossible; Sankey (1993) is cited for discussion of Kuhn's changing accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory-dependence of observation / perceptual incommensurability
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation may be influenced by prior beliefs and experiences so that two scientists can look at the same scene and 'see different things' (e.g., Galileo vs an Aristotelian observing a pendulum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This denies observation as a theory-neutral arbiter and provides another source of incommensurability; Kuhn sometimes uses Gestalt-switch (duck-rabbit) as an analogy though he is cautious about its scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic incommensurability and meaning holism
rubrics_metrics.description: Shifts in meanings of key terms across revolutions (e.g., 'mass' in Newtonian vs Einsteinian contexts) can make translation and point-by-point comparison impossible; meaning holism implies changing one term shifts a network of related terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn invokes holism of theoretical meaning (and extends theory-dependence to observational terms) to argue semantic shifts block straightforward comparison and thus challenge convergent realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of the discovery/justification distinction and rule-governed evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Kuhn rejects the strict distinction between context of discovery and context of justification and denies that acceptability of solutions is determined by fixed rules of rationality; instead, perceived similarity to exemplars governs acceptability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perception of similarity cannot be reduced to rules; this led critics to charge Kuhn with irrationalism, though Kuhn argues similarity-based cognition need not be irrational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mature science vs pre-paradigm criterion (consensus requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mature science has a widespread consensus around paradigmatic problem-solutions, permitting collective progress; a pre-paradigm science lacks such consensus and contains competing schools with differing procedures and metaphysics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consensus on a paradigm unifies theory, methods, language, metaphysics, and instrumentation, enabling cumulative problem-solving and research traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolutionary account of scientific progress (measure of progress)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kuhn favors an evolutionary view where progress is measured by increased problem-solving success and diversification/specialization, not by nearness to an ideal true theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects teleological/convergent-realism accounts; evolutionary analogy allows rejection of extreme relativism while denying convergence on a single true description.
